Corporate Financial Resilience During COVID-19: Sweden vs Cayman Islands

Author

AWADHESKUMAR THAKKAR

Published

October 6, 2025

Code 
# Load each year’s file
load(here("osiris", "osiris_Sweden_2018.rda"))
load(here("osiris", "osiris_Sweden_2019.rda"))
load(here("osiris", "osiris_Sweden_2020.rda"))
load(here("osiris", "osiris_Sweden_2021.rda"))

Introduction

This project explores how firms responded to the economic shock of COVID-19 by analysing financial data from Sweden and the Cayman Islands between 2017 and 2021.

The analysis focuses on revenue, profitability, and sector-level trends to understand resilience patterns across two contrasting economic systems.

Sweden is a diverse and highly competitive economy, mainly focused on goods and manufactures with a growth in service sectors such as information and communications technology (3). According to the OCDE Sweden’s economy is characterised by highly educated workforce, strong institutions, low income inequality and an extensive welfare system that supports productivity and helps individuals participate effectively in the labor market (4). Some of the most famous Swedish companies around the world are Volvo, Ikea, H&M and Spotify (5)

According to the World Bank, the COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2022 triggered the largest global economic crisis of this century (6*). With this report, we aim to investigate how the pandemic impacted the financial performance of Swedish companies. To achieve this, we will use data from OSIRIS database, which provides standardised financial statements of public and private companies worldwide (2). Our analysis will focus on key financial indicators such as liabilities and debt, revenue, total assets, earnings before and after tax, revenues, profit margins and employment. By examining changes in these indicators, we provide an integral analysis of how Sweden’s Corporate sector responded to this crisis and observe any recovery dynamics that might have emerged in the post-pandemic period.

Data description

The dataset covers the period 2017 to 2021, allowing us to compare betwen the pre-pandemic (2017-2019) and pandemic periods (2020 and 2021). The data contains 240 financial variables and around 1800 records per year. The combined dataset includes company identifiers (NAICS classification) and key financial indicators per year.

To ensure the validity of our analysis, we remove duplicated records using firm and year identifiers, variable names are standardised accross years. Outliers will be evaluated through visual inspections (box plots) to detect any potential data entry or reporting anomaly. To ensure that our analysis only focuses on reliable data, we exclude any variable that is considered irrelevant, and retain only variables that contain less than 60% of missing values.

Code 
na_per <- sweden_all %>% 
            is.na() %>% 
            colMeans() %>% 
            sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# contact information is also not useful to keep
# also dont need country information since all are known to be in sweden
useless_cols <- c('Email Address (email)', 
                  'Web Site Address (www)',
                  'FAX - Main Fax Number (fax)',
                  'PHONE - Main Phone Number (phone)',
                  'Country (country)',
                  'Country Code (cntrycde)'
                  )

na_keep <- na_per[na_per < 0.6] %>% names() %>% 
            setdiff(useless_cols)

sweden_dropped <- sweden_all %>% select(all_of(na_keep))

IDA

Sample and coverage overview

Code 
# Uses sweden_all already created above
yr_counts <- sweden_all |>
  dplyr::rename(firm_id = `BvD ID Number (os_id_number)`) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_records   = dplyr::n(),
    n_companies = dplyr::n_distinct(firm_id),
    .by = year
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

kableExtra::kbl(yr_counts, caption = "Records & unique companies by year") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Records & unique companies by year
year n_records n_companies
2017 825 818
2018 874 868
2019 933 926
2020 924 915
2021 911 910

From 2017 to 2021, record counts remained quite consistent, between 825 to 933 per year. Only a few companies have more than one record in a single year since unique-company counts track records closely (gaps of only approx 5–8). Instead of a collapse in coverage, the small rise through 2019 and following slight decline in 2020–2021 are consistent with the slight disruption in reporting throughout the COVID period.

Code 
# Prefer sector_name, fall back to naics_sector
sector_col <- dplyr::case_when(
  "sector_name"  %in% names(sweden_all) ~ "sector_name",
  "naics_sector" %in% names(sweden_all) ~ "naics_sector",
  TRUE ~ NA_character_
)
stopifnot(!is.na(sector_col))

yr_sector_counts <- sweden_all |>
  dplyr::rename(firm_id = `BvD ID Number (os_id_number)`) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sector = tidyr::replace_na(.data[[sector_col]], "Unknown")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_records   = dplyr::n(),
    n_companies = dplyr::n_distinct(firm_id),
    .by = c(year, sector)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year, dplyr::desc(n_records))

yr_sector_distinct_counts <- yr_sector_counts  |>
  select(-n_records) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year,
              values_from = n_companies)

kableExtra::kbl(yr_sector_distinct_counts, caption = "Records & unique companies by year × sector") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

Every year, manufacturing (about 380 businesses) dominates the sample, followed by professional, scientific and technical services, wholesale trade, real estate and rental, and information. Throughout, pandemic-sensitive industries like lodging and food services continue to hold a relatively tiny percentage.

From 2017 to 2021, the sector composition remained surprisingly consistent. Would be ideal to use of sector-stratified views thereafter to avoid the effects of big manufacturing numbers masking smaller sector changes.

Choosing a few important variables to start with. these are subjective. The analysis flow is taken from week 3 slides.

Patterns within total assets and liabilities and debt

Here, some basic investigation into the patterns within the total assets and liabilities is done. First, a simple histogram to see the distribution of assets and liabilities in a single year to get an idea of the distribution.

Code 
# initial investigation will not use a tsibble, only looking at means across all observations in the 5 years
sweden_al_sub <- sweden_ida_sub %>% 
      select(year, total_assets, total_liabilities, sector_name) %>% 
          mutate(l_assets = log10(total_assets + 1),
                 l_liab = log10(total_liabilities+ 1))
# incorporated log statistics based on below observations for easier readability

Separating the data, we now do a simple plot to see if there’s anything obvious, doing a simple histogram (Lecture 1, slide 34).

Code 
# first look at one year to see the distribution
sweden_al_sub %>% filter(year == 2019) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = total_assets)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) + 
  labs(x = "Total Assets")

We can see severe right skewness (which makes sense for financial data), so we will apply a log scale (Lecture 5, slide 28) to make the plot easier to understand and visualise.

Code 
# first look at one year to see the distribution
sweden_al_sub %>% filter(year == 2019) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = total_assets)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) +
  scale_x_log10() + 
  labs(x = "Total Assets")

EDA (with some analysis between)

Looking at this plot, we see a better distribution of the data, where it is relatively normally distributed, so we can use this to generate our means and medians to get a better idea of the distributions (scaling with log and then transforming back) (Lecture 5, slide 29). We also need to add 1 when transforming with the log to ensure we don’t have negative infinity skewing our means. (This was moved a couple chunks up since this will be reused).

Code 
sweden_al_summary <- sweden_al_sub  %>% 
          group_by(year) %>% 
          summarise(`Mean Assets` = 10^mean(l_assets, na.rm = TRUE) - 1,
                    `Median Assets` = 10^median(l_assets, na.rm = TRUE) - 1,
                    `Mean Liabilities` = 10^mean(l_liab, na.rm = TRUE) - 1,
                    `Median Liabilities` = 10^median(l_liab, na.rm = TRUE) - 1)

We see that there is a general increasing trend, although interestingly there appears to be a dip in 2019, although this may be a pattern of the collection methods. To get a better understanding of the distribution, we can use a boxplot to visualise this (Lecture 5, slide 17).

Code

We can see that overall, there is no major shifts across the years, however interestingly there is still an increasing pattern across all the years for both total assets and liabilities, but not a significant shift overall.

To get a better idea of underlying patterns, we can do some stratified visualisation based on the sectors. (Lecture 6, Slide 19)

Code 
sweden_al_sub %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = l_assets)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~sector_name, ncol = 10, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Assets (Logarithmic)"
  )
Code 
sweden_al_sub %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = l_liab)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~sector_name, ncol = 10, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Liabilities and Debt (Logarithmic)"
  )

Looking at this distribution across the different sectors, we can notice there are numerous more interesting changes across the years for many sectors. For example, there are significant spikes in pandemic years (2020 and 2021) in the Accommodation & Food Services and Public Administration. When comparing this to the number of companies across the years, the increase in total assets for Accommodation & Food Services is likely attributed to the poorer performing companies having to shutdown, and only high performing companies remaining. Conversely, the pattern shown in Public Administration is likely due to the relatively large increase in the number of companies in the sector in the pandemic years.

Looking at larger sectors, such as Manufacturing, and Professional, Scientific & Technical services, and Wholesale Trade, there are no significant shifts, although they do have slightly upward trends which aligns with previous inspections of general increases across each year, with no noticeable impact on the total assets or liabilities.

Sectors where this pattern noticeably differs is within the Arts, Entertainment & Recreation, likely due to overall reduced recreational usage, as well as minor drops within the Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing & Hunting and Transportation & Warehousing sectors, which may be attributed to limited outdoor access during pandemic control measures. We also see a noticeable shift in the median assets and liabilities of Education Services, perhaps a result of government or external investment in resources required for remote learning capabilities during the pandemic.

To avoid dropping firms with negative earnings, we have used absolute values of earnings. This allows analysis of earnings magnitudes. the values given above are exponents to base 10.

The proportion of profit- and loss-making firms remained roughly constant over 2017–2021, suggesting no major structural shift in profitability. Now, Using the existing earnings direction categories, we shall compare the median magnitudes of before and after-tax earnings on a log10 scale

Code 
# Add after-tax variables and log transforms
ebt_compare <- ebt_direction %>%
  mutate(
    log_abs_ebt = log10(abs(earnings_before_tax) + 1),
    log_abs_eat = log10(abs(earnings_after_tax)  + 1)
  )

# Summarise by year and direction
summary_simple <- ebt_compare %>%
  group_by(year, direction) %>%
  summarise(
    median_before = median(log_abs_ebt, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_after  = median(log_abs_eat, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot, excluding Zero direction
summary_simple %>%
  filter(direction %in% c("Profit", "Loss")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median_before, color = "Before Tax", group = direction), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median_after,  color = "After Tax",  group = direction),
            linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ direction, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Median log10(|Earnings|) Before vs After Tax by Year",
    x = "Year", y = "Median log10(|Earnings| + 1)",
    color = "Measure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The after-tax line is slightly above the before-tax. profits and losses increased overall in 2021 with greater volatility. some reasons could be post-pandemic recovery, and corporate tax rate cuts in Sweden in the year 2021.

During COVID-19 some companies globally decided to downsize their workforce, then we can explore the number of employees as a proxy of financial health. However in the following summary, we observe that in a pre-pandemic period the average number of employees was lower than in the pandemic period. It is an interesting pattern that should be investigated, based on Lecture 3 slides (slide 46) we can run a t-test to do hypothesis testing.

Code 
# initial investigation will not use a tsibble, only looking at means across all observations in the 5 years
sweden_small <- sweden_ida_sub %>% 
      select(year, employees, profit_margin, naics_sector)

sweden_small <- sweden_small %>% 
  mutate(pandemic_period = case_when(
    year < 2020 ~ 'pre-pandemic',
    year %in% c (2020, 2021, 2022) ~ 'pandemic',
    year >= 2023 ~ 'post-pandemic'
  ))

summary_by_period <- sweden_small %>%
  group_by(pandemic_period) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_profit_margin = mean(profit_margin, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_employees = mean(employees, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_firms = n()
  )

summary_by_period

#week3 slide 46 

tt <- with(sweden_small,
  t.test(
    employees[pandemic_period == "pre-pandemic"],
    employees[pandemic_period == "pandemic"],
    paired = FALSE
  )
)

Based on the results of the t-test we find that there is no significant difference in the means of the number of employees per company between the pandemic and postpandemic periods (p-value =1). This result is an interesting finding as it contradicts the expectation that as a result of lock downs (specially for sectors like mining or manufacture) lockdowns pressured companies to downsize (3). This result can indicate that the trend in Nordic companies, like the ones included in this dataset are resilient or that Sweeden’s pandemic strategy helped companies to retain staff and can lead to further investigation (2).

The broad, rather stable IQR ribbons show disturbance without a structural collapse, indicating heavy-tailed but generally stable dispersion across years.

Now will look at indexed medians which employs dplyr/ggplot2 from Weeks 2 (wrangling) and 5 (summary plots) to compare trends directly on the same scale.

Code 
# Median by year & metric with no residual grouping
medyr <- sweden_all |>
  transmute(
    year,
    total_revenues = as.numeric(`Total revenues (data13004)`),
    gross_sales    = as.numeric(`Gross sales (data13000)`)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(total_revenues, gross_sales),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  group_by(year, metric) |>
  summarise(med = median(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Pulling 2019 baselines per metric
base19 <- medyr |>
  filter(year == 2019) |>
  rename(baseline = med) |>
  select(metric, baseline)

# Joining baseline and computing index (falls back to first non-missing if 2019 is NA/missing)
med_idx <- medyr |>
  left_join(base19, by = "metric") |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  mutate(
    baseline = ifelse(is.na(baseline),
                      med[which.min(abs(year - 2019))],  # fallback baseline
                      baseline),
    idx_2019 = 100 * med / baseline
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(med_idx, aes(x = year, y = idx_2019, colour = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Indexed medians (2019 = 100)",
       y = "Median index", x = "Year", colour = NULL)

Gross sales and total revenues move nearly in unison, with a distinct decline in 2020 (~93–94) and a significant rebound in 2021 (~111–112), according to the indexed-median plot (2019 = 100). The dashed line at 100 serves as a marker for changes in relation to the pre-pandemic baseline, and values are based on raw medians with na.rm=TRUE.

We will now compare gross sales to total revenues as a ratio by year to verify consistency between the two metrics. By plotting log10(gross_sales/total_revenues), we may determine if typical firms sit close to equality and how dispersion varies over time. This places “parity” at 0 (i.e., 1×). Thisemploys distributions with modified scales in ggplot2 (Week 5–6).

Code 
ratio_df <- sweden_all |>
transmute(
year,
total_revenues = as.numeric(`Total revenues (data13004)`),
gross_sales    = as.numeric(`Gross sales (data13000)`)
) |>

# keep comparable values
filter(!is.na(total_revenues), !is.na(gross_sales),
total_revenues > 0, gross_sales >= 0) |>
mutate(
ratio      = gross_sales / total_revenues,
log_ratio  = log10(ratio)           # 0 on this scale ⇔ ratio = 1
)

ggplot(ratio_df, aes(x = factor(year), y = log_ratio)) +
geom_violin(fill = "grey85", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.6, trim = TRUE) +
geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
scale_y_continuous(
name = "log10(Gross sales / Total revenues)",
breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
labels = c("0.1×","0.32×","1×","3.2×","10×")
) +
labs(
title = "How close are gross sales to total revenues?",
x = "Year"
)

As expected, most firms’ gross sales are near to their total revenues as the violins sit tightly around 0 on the log scale (≈1×) each year. Dispersion has a slight right tail and is relatively constant between years.

Conclusions

Changes in coverage are unlikely to be the driving force behind patterns as Sweden’s business sample and sector mix remained consistent from 2017 to 2021. With only slight year-to-year variation, balance-sheet size (assets and liabilities) showed a gentle rising trend, suggesting that businesses mostly preserved their scale and financing ability under COVID. Flow metrics (gross sales and total revenues) exhibit a typical decline in 2020 and a distinct comeback in 2021, usually above 2019 medians. IQRs stay broad but stable, which is consistent with heavy-tailed distributions rather than a midpoint collapse. Throughout the years, the gross-sales/total-revenues ratio remained consistently below 1, indicating that the revenue composition did not significantly change (i.e., there was no significant shift towards non-sales income).

As the size of both profits and losses increased in 2021, earnings had the strongest pandemic “signature,” suggesting a more divided recovery with distinct winners and poor performers. Comparing headcounts before and after the epidemic revealed no statistically significant decline, suggesting worker hoarding, resilience, and/or supporting policy settings. According to sector opinions, public administration increased as pandemic-sensitive areas (like lodging and food) moved more, while major sectors (like manufacturing, professional services, and wholesale) stayed the same.

The pandemic caused a brief, moderate revenue shock in 2020, a robust recovery in 2021, increased earnings volatility, and no widespread downsizing, or stress without systemic harm. The remaining concerns which should be considered include survivorship effects, big tails, and zeros/negatives; sector-specific drills and deeper panel models which would improve attribution.
